detail: supported

Ambient Volume Illumination is a family of local illumination algorithms for direct volume rendering that approximates light transport based on the local "ambient region" of each data point, aiming to reproduce phenomenological illumination effects for interactive performance [S1, unofficial].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S1]. The source explicitly states that 'Ambient Volume Illumination' discusses illumination algorithms for direct volume rendering based on the 'ambient region' of each point. It confirms the aim to reproduce important illumination effects on a 'phenomenological level' for 'interactive performance'. It also details the use of ambient occlusion for local shadows and ambient scattering for complex light interactions, matching the specific technical details in the claim.
supported
The concept was introduced in the paper "Ambient Volume Illumination" published in IEEE Computing in Science and Engineering in 2016 [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the paper 'Ambient Volume Illumination' was published in 'IEEE Computing in Science and Engineering' in 2016. It also describes the concept as illumination algorithms for direct volume rendering based on the ambient region, aiming to reproduce important illumination effects for interactive performance, which aligns with the claim.
supported

What sets it apart from its siblings is the explicit use of ambient scattering to simulate complex light-matter interactions, providing stronger visual cues for spatial arrangement than ambient occlusion alone [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that ambient scattering is used to simulate complex light-matter interactions and provides stronger visual cues for spatial arrangement than ambient occlusion. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly supports this: it mentions that 'ambient scattering can be employed to simulate more complex interactions of light with matter' and that 'ambient scattering provides more visual cues for spatial depth... compared to ambient occlusion, which has difficulties conveying spatial arrangement.'
supported

It emerged from ongoing research in volume visualization focused on developing simplified optical models that reproduce important illumination effects on a phenomenological level to achieve interactive performance and simpler parameter control compared to accurate global illumination [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that ongoing research in volume visualization focuses on developing simplified optical models to reproduce important illumination effects on a phenomenological level for interactive performance and simpler parameter control compared to accurate global illumination. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Ongoing research in volume visualization focuses on the development of simplified optical models that can reproduce the most important illumination effects that help improve perception, but on a phenomenological level to obtain interactive performance and simpler control of the parameters compared to accurate global illumination.' This matches the claim fact-for-fact.
supported
It is used in direct volume rendering to help users perceive spatial depth, discover cavities, and identify salient structures in volumetric data sets [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that ambient occlusion helps 'perceive spatial depth' and 'discover cavities' (Source [S1] passages). It also states that ambient scattering helps 'perceive the shape of volumetric structures' and provides cues for 'spatial depth'. Furthermore, the text contrasts the emission-absorption model, where it is 'difficult to visually identify salient structures due to missing illumination', with illumination models (like Blinn-Phong and ambient scattering) that help perceive structures and depth. Thus, the claim that these techniques are used to help users perceive spatial depth, discover cavities, and identify salient structures is fully supported by the text.
unsupported
Usually, a simple absorption and emission model is used because it is relatively cheap to evaluate and gives good enough results [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that a simple absorption and emission model is used because it is 'relatively cheap to evaluate and gives good enough results.' However, the evidence explicitly states that with the emission-absorption model, 'it is difficult to visually identify salient structures due to missing illumination' and that perception of spatial depth is limited. While the text mentions that ongoing research focuses on simplified models to obtain interactive performance (cheap evaluation), it does not support the part of the claim that the absorption and emission model gives 'good enough results'; rather, it presents it as a baseline with significant visual deficiencies compared to ambient scattering.
supported
It solves the problem of poor spatial depth perception and feature occlusion inherent in simple emission-absorption models by introducing local shadows and indirect light cues [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that ambient occlusion helps 'perceive spatial depth' and 'discover cavities' (addressing depth perception). It also notes that ambient scattering provides 'directional shadows and indirect light' (addressing local shadows and indirect light cues). Furthermore, the text contrasts these methods with the 'emission-absorption model,' stating that with the latter, it is 'difficult to visually identify salient structures due to missing illumination' and that even Blinn-Phong has 'limited' spatial depth perception, implying the emission-absorption model has inherent difficulties with these aspects. The claim accurately summarizes the benefits of the introduced methods (ambient occlusion and scattering) over the simple emission-absorption model as described in the text.
